chapters.title: Chapter 5: Trading Mechanics, Risk and Tax

lessons.title: Position Sizing and Stop Losses for Currency Traders

children.text: Two traders, Rhea and Varun, each start with ₹3,00,000 and trade the same EUR/USD futures on NSE with the same strategy. Over a bad month, both suffer ten losing trades in a row, which happens even to good strategies. Rhea risks 1% of her account per trade and ends the streak with about ₹2,71,000. Varun risks 10% per trade and is left with about ₹1,05,000, needing to nearly triple his money just to get back to zero. Same market, same entries, same exits. The only difference was position size. This lesson shows you how to size every trade from the loss you can accept, where to place a stop-loss, and why the maths of risk matters more than being right.

body.text: Decide how much you are willing to lose before you decide how much to buy. Position size should come from your stop-loss distance and a fixed slice of your capital, never from how confident you feel or how much margin is available.

children.text: Step 1: Fix Your Risk per Trade

markDefs.definition: The amount of money you stand to lose on a trade if the stop-loss is hit. Often called 1R. Profits are then measured as multiples of R.

children.text: Professional traders start with a rule: risk only a small, fixed percentage of the account on any single trade, typically 0.5% to 2%. That amount is your
risk per trade
, or 1R. Rhea's account is ₹3,00,000 and she uses 1%, so 1R = ₹3,000. Every trade she takes is built so that if it goes wrong, she loses about ₹3,000 and no more.

body.title: Account Value During a 10-Trade Losing Streak (% of starting capital)

children.text: After ten straight losses at 1%, the account is still above 90%, and a 10.6% gain gets it back. At 10% per trade, only about 35% remains, and it needs a gain of about 187% to recover. Losing streaks are not a sign that a strategy is broken. They are a normal feature of trading. Position sizing decides whether you survive them.
Step 2: Place the Stop Where the Idea Is Proven Wrong

markDefs.definition: The most recent clear low point on a chart before prices rose again. Traders often place stops for long positions just below it.
Average True Range. The average size of a currency's daily price range over a period, commonly 14 days. Used to set stops wide enough to survive normal noise.

children.text: A stop-loss should not be a random number of pips or a rupee amount you picked because it feels comfortable. It belongs at the price where your reason for the trade no longer holds. For a long trade, that is often just below a recent
swing low
, with a small buffer. It should also be wider than normal daily noise, which traders measure with
ATR
. The stop comes first. The position size follows from it.

body.title: EUR/USD Futures: Rhea's Setup (illustrative daily candles)

children.text: Rhea plans to buy at 1.1600. The swing low on Day 3 is 1.1552. If EUR/USD falls below that, the higher low her trade depends on has failed. She places her stop at 1.1545, seven pips below the swing low as a buffer. Her stop distance is 55 pips.

body.title: Using ATR to check if a stop is too tight

children.text: Suppose EUR/USD's 14-day ATR is 60 pips, meaning it typically covers about 60 pips between its daily high and low. A 15-pip stop would be hit by ordinary noise most days, even if the trade idea is right. Many traders set stops at least 1 to 2 times ATR away, or confirm that a chart-based stop is not much tighter than one ATR.

Rhea's 55-pip stop is close to one ATR, which is reasonable for a trade held a few days. If ATR doubled during a volatile week, she would need a wider stop, and therefore fewer lots to keep the same ₹3,000 risk. Volatility changes position size, not risk per trade.
Step 3: Calculate the Position Size

body.latex: \text{Lots} = \frac{\text{Risk per trade (₹)}}{\text{Stop distance} \times \text{Rupee value of that distance per lot}}
body.caption: Always round down to a whole number of lots
Rupee value of moves per lot on Indian exchanges (at USD/INR 95.50 for cross-currency pairs)
headers: One pip, tick or paisa is

stats.label: Loss per lot at the stop

body.title: How many lots?
body.prompt: Rhea risks ₹3,000 per trade. Her stop is 55 pips away, and each lot loses ₹525.25 if the stop is hit. How many whole lots should she buy?
body.explanation: ₹3,000 ÷ ₹525.25 = 5.71 lots. Round down to 5 lots, so her actual risk is 5 × ₹525.25 = ₹2,626.25, just under her 1% limit. Rounding up to 6 would risk ₹3,151.50, breaking her own rule. Notice she is not using anywhere near the 90 lots her margin would allow.

body.text: Never widen a stop-loss once a trade is open because the price is getting close to it. That single habit turns a planned 1R loss into a 3R or 5R loss, and it is the most common way disciplined sizing breaks down. You can move a stop closer to lock in profit. You should never move it further away to avoid taking a loss.

children.text: Step 4: Check the Reward and the Expectancy

markDefs.definition: The average amount you expect to make or lose per trade over many trades, given your win rate and the size of your average win and loss.

children.text: Rhea's target is 1.1710, 110 pips above entry, twice her 55-pip risk. That is a reward-to-risk ratio of 2. With a 2R target, she breaks even over time if she wins just one trade in three. What matters is not any single trade, but her
expectancy
across many trades.

body.latex: \text{Expectancy per trade (in R)} = (\text{Win rate} \times \text{Average win}) - (\text{Loss rate} \times \text{Average loss})
body.caption: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + reward-to-risk ratio)
Expectancy for different win rates with a 2R target and 1R stop, before costs

body.title: Break-even win rate
body.prompt: Varun uses a stop of 40 pips and a target of 60 pips on every trade, a reward-to-risk ratio of 1.5. Ignoring costs, what win rate does he need just to break even? Enter a percentage.
body.explanation: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + 1.5) = 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.40, or 40%. Check: 0.40 × 1.5 minus 0.60 × 1 = 0.60 minus 0.60 = 0. After brokerage, charges and slippage, he needs to win meaningfully more than 40% to make money.

body.text: Costs quietly eat expectancy. If each round trip costs Rhea about ₹60 in brokerage and charges, that is about 0.02R on a ₹2,626 risk, small enough to live with. But a trader who risks only ₹300 per trade pays the same ₹60, which is 0.2R, enough to turn a 40% win rate strategy from profitable to break-even. Very small positions and very frequent trading make costs a much larger share of every trade.

children.text: Good Stops vs Bad Stops

body.title: What separates a useful stop-loss from a harmful one

columns.label: Good stop
points: Placed where the trade idea is proven wrong
Wider than normal daily noise, checked against ATR
Set before entry, with position size calculated from it
Placed a few pips away from obvious round numbers where many orders cluster
Never moved further away once the trade is live

columns.label: Bad stop
points: A rupee amount chosen because it feels comfortable
So tight that ordinary noise hits it
Added after the trade has already moved against you
Sitting exactly on 1.1500 or another round number
Widened or cancelled when the price gets close

body.text: Hedgers generally should not use stop-losses on their hedges. When Karthik's EUR/INR futures lose money, his euro payment is getting cheaper at the same time. A stop that closes the futures would remove his protection exactly when the currency is moving, turning a hedge back into an open risk. For hedgers, the equivalent discipline is sizing the hedge to the real exposure and keeping enough cash for mark-to-market.

body.title: Sizing when volatility rises
body.question: EUR/USD's daily range doubles during a volatile week, so Rhea widens her chart-based stop from 55 pips to 110 pips. Keeping her risk at 1% of capital, what should happen to her position size?
options: She should remove the stop instead
body.explanation: Each lot now loses 110 × $0.10 × 95.50 = ₹1,050.50 at the stop. ₹3,000 ÷ ₹1,050.50 = 2.86, so she rounds down to 2 lots. A wider stop means fewer lots, keeping the rupee risk the same.

body.title: The revenge trade
body.scenario: Varun has ₹3,00,000 and has just lost three EUR/USD trades in a row, down ₹27,000 because he risked 3% each time. Frustrated, he decides to "win it back" with one trade. He buys 60 lots at 1.1600 with no stop-loss, saying he will close "when it comes back." By the next afternoon, EUR/USD has fallen to 1.1480 after a surprise European Central Bank statement.
body.prompt: Calculate Varun's loss on the 60-lot trade at 1.1480 using USD/INR 95.50, state it as a share of his remaining capital, and identify every risk-management mistake he made. What should his process have been after the losing streak?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Loss: 120 pips × $0.10 × 60 lots = $720. At 95.50, that is ₹68,760.
2. His capital after the first three losses was ₹2,73,000. The single trade lost about 25% of that, taking his total drawdown to about ₹95,760, or 32% of his starting ₹3,00,000.
3. Mistakes: risking 3% per trade to begin with; sizing the new trade from emotion instead of a stop; trading with no stop-loss at all; using a huge position of 60 lots; and relying on the price "coming back," which is hope, not a plan.
4. Recovery maths: from about ₹2,04,240 he now needs a gain of about 47% just to return to ₹3,00,000.
5. Better process: treat a losing streak as normal; keep risk at 1% or cut it to 0.5% until confidence returns; take a break after a set number of losses; and only take trades with a predefined stop, target and position size calculated in advance.

body.title: Your pre-trade plan
steps: Confirm the contract is one you are allowed to trade: cross-currency without an exposure, rupee pairs only to hedge.
Write down the entry price and the reason for the trade.
Set the stop-loss where that reason fails, and check it against ATR.
Calculate 1R as a fixed percentage of capital, such as 1%.
Calculate lots from 1R and the stop distance, rounding down.
Set a target and confirm the reward-to-risk ratio is worth it after costs.
Place the stop order at the same time as the entry, and do not widen it later.

body.title: The break-even rule
body.textWithBlank: With a reward-to-risk ratio of 2, the break-even win rate before costs is about ___%.
body.explanation: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + 2) = 33.3%. A trader targeting twice their risk can be wrong two times out of three and still break even before costs.

cards.definition: The rupee amount you lose if a trade hits its stop. Usually a fixed 0.5% to 2% of capital.
Lots = risk per trade ÷ (stop distance × rupee value per lot). Round down.
Average True Range, the typical daily range of a currency, used to check a stop is not too tight.
Target distance divided by stop distance. A 110-pip target with a 55-pip stop is 2 to 1.
Win rate × average win minus loss rate × average loss, measured in R per trade.

points: Fix risk per trade as a small percentage of capital, typically 0.5% to 2%, before choosing a position size.
Place stops where the trade idea is proven wrong and wider than normal noise, then size the position from that stop.
Lots = risk per trade ÷ (stop distance × rupee value per lot), always rounded down.
Wider stops mean fewer lots; volatility changes position size, not risk.
Expectancy, not individual wins, decides long-term results. A 2R target breaks even at a 33.3% win rate before costs.
Never widen a stop once a trade is live, and never trade without one when you have no underlying exposure.
Hedgers size to the real exposure and generally avoid stops, because a stop would remove protection when it is needed most.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Chart data, prices, costs and win rates are illustrative. Position sizing and stop-losses reduce risk but do not eliminate it, and stops can be filled at worse prices during gaps. Rupee-pair derivatives may be used only to hedge genuine currency exposures.
